children.title: Geometry as part of the real world

blocks.text: The word geometry comes from the Greek words Geo which has to do with Earth (The Greek goddess Gea) and metry from metrein which has to do with measurement.
Montessori’s geometry has its roots in Children’s House but there it is not called geometry.

Geometry is the science that treats of the size and shape of things. It helps us to understand how it can be found in a hidden form in the Children’s House where the children start handling shapes with the age of 3. They are exploring the shapes and sizes. At such a young age the direct aim is the visual discrimination and the indirect aim is the preparation for geometry.

In the 0-3 years age group the children absorb the shapes from the environment as they are “sensory motor explorers”. They are exploring the world also from a geometric point of view without the need of special materials.
The more abstract the approach is, the older the age has to be and the more concrete the younger the age should be.

When we talk about shapes we can make a distinction of two classes of shapes: two dimensional and three dimensional. In life everything that exists is three dimensional, but the dimensions might not always be very obvious.

We tend first to observe in everything that surrounds us the two-dimensional shapes even if these are contained in a three-dimensional object. Everything that exists and we can see, it is made of shapes. If we look at the shape and size of the things that surround us we can find the geometric aspect of life.

“In our work we have given a name to this part of the mind which is built up with exactitude... we call it “the mathematical mind.” I take the term from Pascal ... who said that man’s mind was mathematical by nature, and that
knowledge and progress come from accurate observation.” Maria Montessori – Absorbent Mind.
The human environment it is called super nature by Maria Montessori.
The first part of the Introduction can be called Geometry as part of the real world.
We want the children to observe and to discover the shapes in the marvelous nature that surrounds them.
In Children’s House we can talk about shapes and in Elementary we can talk about figures.

The fundamental figures in the Montessori geometry are the equilateral triangle, circle and the square. The triangle (“the constructor”) is the polygon with the smallest number of sides. Any polygon can be broken down into triangles. The square (“the measurer”) is related to the measurement of areas, as the area is calculated in square meters. Finding the area, is finding how many squares make that area. The circle (“the calculator”) is used for calculating the angles. Circle is the limit
f the regular polygon and where the sides had shrunk to a point.
When a polygon has equal sides and angles we call it a regular polygon.

children.title: Hidden geometry in Children’s House

blocks.text: In the first plane of development there are different sensitive periods:
Sensitive period for movement
Sensitive period for language
Sensitive period for the senses
Sensitive period for order
In the Children’s House there are materials for the training and refinement of the senses:
Sight
Hearing
Smell
Taste
Touch:
Tactile (for textures)
Thermic (for temperature)
Baric (for weight)
Stereognostic (a combination of the touch senses to perceive an object)
Geometry is the science that treats of the size and shape of things. The sense of sight gives us information about colour, shape and size.

The sensorial materials that have to do with shape and size are: geometry cabinet, geometric solids and the constructive triangles. These sensorial materials provide an indirect preparation for geometry. Most of the concepts that we treat in the geometry in Elementary find its roots in the Children’s House.
The benefits of educating the senses are that the children can have a physical
experience with the materials which gives the children a refinement of the senses
and helps them to discriminate better the differences: the big contrasts but also
the very small differences. A human being with educated senses is a better
bserver and to those who are able to observe more carefully, the world
becomes a richer place.
Ordering the impressions with the help of the material in Children’s House, it brings
rder to the mind. An ordered mind becomes a sharp mind as the information is
classified.
We are using the sensorial materials also to identify any possible problems or deviations from which the child might suffer, as the sensorial materials offer exactness.

children.title: Elementary Geometry

blocks.text: Things change from one plane to the other and also the way we thing about geometry in the Elementary where we can call geometry psychogeometry. What stays constant are the principles which stay true for all the education plans and for all the ages.

children.title: Leading principles of the Montessori approach

blocks.text: Maria Montessori was interested to find the way the child develops and from there to create a curriculum. For her the development was always in the center another way to say that nature has to be respected.

Doctor Maria Montessori prepared an environment, without this environment the child will only depend on the adult for learning. This environment holds the “motives for activity” and is using the materials to help the children reach abstraction spontaneously like a discovery. At different ages the environment has to change to respect the development of the child.

The children in the Elementary classroom are of mixed age with a span of a minimum of 3 years. Without mixed ages there is not a Montessori school. The children should have access to the other classes 3-6 or 9-12 if the children are in the 6-9 classroom. An open doors approach as the education should not be limited by age, freedom of movement and freedom of choice are important principles of Montessori education. The children should have access to all the materials. Other benefit for the mixed age environment is that it reduces the pressure on the children and the competition between themselves.

No timetables, so the children can work with a material as long as they want. This a very good approach as the subconscious mind will reveal itself if there is an interest in that particular subject. The knowledge accumulated in this way will emerge as conscious understanding. Not having timetables allows the children to organize their work time and choose on what they would like to work.

Abstraction is the result of the individual experience, as we cannot benefit from other persons abstraction. The children have to reach abstraction through their work and experience. The individual has to reach abstraction spontaneously. The time necessary to reach abstraction will vary from one individual to other.

Interest in certain activities are determined more by the sensitivities of the age than what the teacher is doing. If we take in consideration the natural development of the children we can easily understand that the interests
f the child are based on the sensitivities of the age.

The indirect aim is always present in all the materials that Dr. Maria Montessori prepared for the children as it is a preparation for the future, or we can describe it as a training of the subconscious.

The material itself reduces the complexity and divides it in easier concepts, which allow the children to learn very clearly. This can be called the isolation of difficulty. The process of abstraction is broken down into various steps, offering the children different levels of knowledge as they progress with the time. A way to distribute the knowledge in such a way ensures that the knowledge will be appropriate and of interest for that age.

Maria Montessori said that the elementary geometry is all about discovery and a preparation of the mind – not a systematic study. It can be described as a gymnasium for the mind. At this age the children are able to make their own discoveries, the theorems itself are not interesting meanwhile finding it themselves while possessing the words necessary are remarkable achievements for the second plane child. Once the children start on this path they will conquer the rest by themselves without setting boundaries. The use of the material through manipulation can clarify to a child concepts which maybe the adult cannot even do it. It is easier to give the language to the children when they are in the sensitive period for it so later the children can use it for going on with the other activities that are of their interest.

Maria Montessori used observation understand better the children’s sensitive periods and their interests at a specific age. When a sensitive period is over the child loses its interest for an activity for which at an earlier stage he had an enormous interest. This lead to the understanding of how to create an environment for the child’s interest and how this environment should change when the child grows.

Mario Montessori said that when the subjects are distributed for the appropriate age, when the children are free and when they are free to make the passage to abstraction at their own peace, the children show a lot of enthusiasm for learning that subject. They also might appear precocious for learning that subject.

children.title: Geometry cabinet
Introduction of the geometry cabinet

blocks.text: From an elementary point of view in the first drawer of the geometry cabinet the shapes are ordered by the number of sides. The drawers in the cabinet follow the same pattern from top to bottom. In the triangles drawer, on the first row the triangles are ordered by the type of the sides (scalene, isosceles and equilateral) and on the second row are ordered by the type of the angle (right angled, obtuse angled and acute angled). The equilateral triangle goes always last as it is the “perfect triangle”. The right angled triangle goes first as we always use it as a point of reference for the other two angle types. In the rectangles drawer we find the square at the end, by this showing first how a rectangle can grow to become a square and also leaving at the end the “perfect rectangle”. Arithmetic is used to help geometry and the other way round in Elementary education. (E.g. golden beads used to form rectangles) In the drawer of the circles we find that the circles are ordered from the smallest to the biggest. For the Children’s House, the order of the shapes can be different as we are interested in the sensorial aspect of the shapes. For the order of the drawers we can use first the circles drawer, the rectangles drawer, the triangle drawer, the polygon’s drawer, and the miscellaneous drawer. In the drawers we start with the perfect figure (big circle, square, equilateral triangle).
Three period lessons (according to Camillo Grazzini)
First period: Offering a gift
Second period: Acceptance of the gift If the child is not right with one of the terms, we can go back to the first period or try again another day Third period: The return of the gift

Maria Montessori said that we should limit the amount of language used during the three period lessons. In Elementary we still use the three period lessons but not in such a clear format. During the language lessons for the geometrical shapes we should always encourage the child to use his hands to trace and learn through his senses as well.
After the child has been working with a drawer he can increase and work with two drawers, then three drawers till he is working with all the drawers.
Cards

There are three sets of cards, each with 30 cards corresponding to the shapes in the geometry cabinets. The sets differentiate themselves as in the first set we can find the filled shapes as in the cabinet. In the second there is a representation of the shape with a thick outline and in the third set we can find a representation
f the shape with a thin outline – the perimeter of the shape.

The children will start working with the cards, with one set a time corresponding to one drawer. The cards are a work of matching of the shape from the cabinet with the shape on the card. Control of error for the cards: The child’s eyesight to find out if he is right or wrong.

Use cards from the three sets and the child has to match the inset to the cards. Another variation is to lay down all the insets and cards, remove one card and the child must find which one is missing.
Environment game
Use the environment to explore spontaneously shapes that are present around child.
Written language
We can use labels for the names of the shapes. So the children can practice matching the label with the insets. The first step of reading is reading words. “Reading is hearing with your eyes.”

children.title: Presentation tray – Children’s House

blocks.text: At the beginning there are going to be 3 contrasting shapes presented to the child. During the presentation the guide doesn’t speak and uses his index and middle fingers to trace the shapes and the insets. The movements are precise and clear for the child to observe them. Once the guide’s presentation is over he invites the child to try by himself.
There are two stage in which the material should be introduced: 1. Stage of attempts – contrasting shapes. 2. Methodical observation - similar shapes.

For the first the period we can have a variation on how we present the figures depending on their special features: length of the side for the rectangles drawers, starting with the common part of their names “gon” and its etymology for the polygons with more than four sides. For the circle’s drawer the children already know the name so we can show them how a circle grows like a rectangle grew to become a square. For the miscellaneous drawer we can separate the oval, ellipse and a curvilinear triangle and on the side we bring a circle to help us with the visualization for the children. Another presentation can be the trapezoid and the rhombus. The flowers can be presented together, all three (first one doesn’t have a proper name, quatrefoil and epicycloid).

children.title: Constructive triangles
Introduction

blocks.text: Compared with the geometry cabinet the work with the constructive triangles is quite different. It is like a passage from a world of shapes to a place where the children can build shapes. If the children are not interested in the geometry cabinet, it is not a big concern as they will have the opportunity to work with the shapes while using the constructive triangles. In the Children’s House this is a sensorial material. It is a more advanced material then the geometry cabinet as it doesn’t isolate just one quality.

blocks.text: Euler’s theorem to show the relationship between the number of faces and vertices. children.title: Conclusion for the Children’s House geometry

blocks.text: At the beginning of the 20th century there has been a lot of criticism due to the fact that too much geometry and knowledge was given to the young children instead of giving them more play time.
In the Children’s House the children can observe the others as long as they want if they do it respectfully. In the Elementary there is freedom as well but a freedom
f choice.

While referring back to the young children, they are constantly in contact with geometry in the form of the environment that surrounds them in the daily life. If we can talk about harm then it should be about a system in which the children are forced to do activities, which is not the case for Children’s House.

In Children’s house the children work with beautiful precise materials that attract them to do manipulate them and explore how it works. In the Sensorial area the geometry comes as a sensorial experience in Children’s House. It allows the children to explore the different proprieties of the objects at a subconscious level allowing these impressions to become conscious at a later time in life. The repetition of the manipulation of the material create long lasting experiences in the subconscious mind. As said before at an older age the children will be surprised of discovering that so many concepts are familiar and perceive them as pleasant and might even say “personal”. If there is any enthusiasm later in life for geometry it might be as a consequence of these previous subconscious experiences.

The indirect preparation is a training of the subconscious mind which will enable the child to learn through discovery and not only in a direct way as in a traditional classroom. As well a way to prepare himself by acquiring individual pieces of knowledge that later the child can connect and use to understand more complex concepts.
If in the work there are some complex concepts appearing there is a need of synthesis, breaking down in simpler concepts in order to understand and order the information.

When the children come, even if they came from Children’s House there is no guarantee that all they will have the same amount of knowledge. It is important to observe, understand the level what’s the child’s level and pick up from there.

children.title: Presentation of the measurement of the angles
The story of the star

blocks.text: We want to find more about angles. What kind of angles do you know? , What kind of parts do you know?

Today we want to know more about sizes. Can you order the angles you know from smallest to largest? This doesn’t tell you exactly how large the angle is though does it. To know what the size is exactly we need to know how to measure the size exactly. We need to know how to measure an angle. A cup for measuring flour not for angles, a ruler it for measuring lines not angles. To find out what we do use for angles I will tell you a story. The story is called the story of a star.

This is a very old story, we have to go back a long time ago to a place far far away called Mesopotamia. We are going to have to imagine this. Long, long ago there were people living there. These people were called the Sumerians. They lived so long ago that we speak of their society as the very first civilization. But what did they do? Many were famers, some were rulers and some were scribes, which means that their profession was to write and read. Only a few people were scribes which tells us only a few people could write and read in this time. The Sumerians we are interested in are the priests. In those days the Priests were also the scientists. They were always trying to discover things or get to know things, they didn’t make their own food, make their own clothing or help to build the temples. Everything the Priest needed was given to them by other people. They

could spend all their time to be Priests, they studied, observed and made calculations. What did they observe though? Above all they observed the sky, the heavens by day and by night. They were able to produce a calendar. A calendar is a way of looking at the whole year so that you can organise the whole year. When people first started to farm it was very useful as they needed to know when to sow the seeds and when to harvest, the calendar would help them. It also regulated the lives of the people, their daily lives and religious lives, like knowing when the holy days were.

Now we want to imagine these priests observing the skies. They watched the sun, they watched the moon, but most of all, they observed the stars. They are also known as the star gazers. They observed the stars in their groups, a group of stars is called a constellation. They observed the constellations and observed the stars individually, they watched and recorded all the movements of the heavenly bodies. Let’s imagine these priests on the roof of their temples observing the stars at night, night after night they gazed at the stars. They discovered that some stars would appear on the horizon. And they would move night after night through the sky in an arc. The star would appear then the next night the star would appear a little higher in the night sky. It is as if the star is making a journey through the sky. Eventually as they kept watching, they saw the star disappear. If they had waited long enough the star would reappear and they saw this over and over. Do we know what we call these people who watch the stars? Astronomers, these priests were really astronomers. They were really interested in this one star, it shone very brightly in the night sky. After they had watched this one star for a very, very, very long time. They calculated that it took 360 days for the star to appear, disappear and then reappear again. So that means to make a full cycle, they calculated 360 nights for the complete journey - the full cycle. So they decided that a year was 360 days on the calendar. Is that right? Is a year 360 day? Yes or no. 365 days, 5 hours, 48 minutes and 46 seconds is how long the exact year is. Our calendars just show 365 days usually. So they made a terrible mistake but to be fair they discovered their mistake themselves and they added 5 days to their calendar and those 5 days they added later they considered to be holy days or sacred days. We have to remember that they did not have special instruments that we do, no telescopes, no recording instruments, just their eyes, their hands to record and they found their own mistake.

What did I say was their original year? It was 360, before they realized their mistake. We kept the original 360 days to measure our angles except we don’t say 360 days we say 360 degrees. 360 degrees stands for the whole journey for that special bright star.
The guide makes a circle with the head when talking about the 360 degrees and the journey of the star.

blocks.text: The guide brings the Montessori protractor and says let us imagine that in the priest was located in the center. Let us suppose that the star when he first observed it, it was at 0 degrees.
One day passed and the star is at 1, two days passed and the star is at 2
and so on but after the 90 days the star was not visible anymore. The
priest had to wait until the 270th day to see the star again. On the 271st day the star was here, and on the 272nd the star was here.
The guide shows that the full journey of the star is a complete rotation – 360 days/360 degrees.
The guide introduces the name of the instrument: “This instrument it is called a protractor”

The guide says that he would like to find out which figure is a convex closed curve figure and which is a concave closed curve figure. For this he needs to make a test

children.title: Story of the right-angled scalene triangle, build a right-angled scalene triangle and write the prepared label

blocks.text: The guide invites the children to build a right-angled scalene triangle.
The child can try for a few minutes.

The guide says that this is a very special triangle and that he is going to tell him a story, which will help him to learn how to build the triangle: This story is from a long time ago based in a country called Egypt. In Egypt there is a river called the Nile. The river would flood every year back then, with everything going well it would flood and
verflow the banks, this would be good for the farmers as it would

water their fields with very rich nutrient waters. It did mean the boundaries were destroyed, as it would wipe it out thought. There was a special person called lancaverier who would fix the banks along the river. He would walk around very proud and did not carry anything as his followers would carry everything for him, they would even carry his sandals. He had a special rope, a rope who would help him measure. The Egyptians used this special rope when building the pyramids as well. The rope had knots or marks at equal intervals. They discovered that if three people would hold the rope; one person holding the start of the rope, another at 3 knots distance and a third person at 4 knots distance and the first one would hold also the end

f the rope then they have made a triangle. The important angle that we can see is a right-angled. This is scalene because of the three different sides. What the Egyptians had made was a right-angle scalene triangle. They were interested in the right angle of the triangle, they called it a rope stretcher triangle but in fact it was a right-angled scalene triangle.

children.title: Concluding presentation for the quadrilaterals (A portrait gallery)

blocks.text: Geometry sticks
Supply box for geometry
Paper slips for writing

children.title: Presentation of the “Concluding presentation”
Bring the quadrilaterals from the geometry cabinet

blocks.text: The guide asks the children to bring the quadrilaterals and selects the 7 required quadrilaterals and leaves the others that are not required now.

The guide tells the children this story: Did you know that once upon a time many European countries had noble had families but nobles traced their ancestry back many generations. They not only know who their ancestors are, but they also have portraits
f these ancestors. They had portrait galleries with all their ancestors in

their residences. Today we want to look at the portrait gallery of our noble family of quadrilaterals. Who was the quadrilateral that started it all, the great-great grandfather of the quadrilaterals? The common quadrilateral
he was the first one in the family.
[Place the common quadrilateral at the top – center; place the 1st generation card]
The common quadrilateral gave birth to another branch that we can think
f as the “parallel sides branch” – the first one in this branch is the
trapezium.
[Place 1 arrow pointing down/left and the trapezium; place the 2nd generation card]
The trapezium gave rise to even a more special member of the family – the common parallelogram – who has 2 pairs of parallel sides. This is the third generation.
[Place 1 arrow pointing down/left and the common parallelogram; place the 3rd generation card]
Meantime the common quadrilateral gave birth to another branch, the
ne with the equal sides. A kite has 2 pairs of equal adjacent sides – he is
here in the 3rd generation.
[Place 2 arrow pointing down/right and the kite; at the height of the 3rd generation card]
The common parallelogram gave birth to another special member: the rectangle. The rectangle is the 4th generation.
[Place 1 arrow pointing down/left and the rectangle; place the 4th generation card]

Meantime there is a very special member where the 2 branches of the families come together: the rhombus. The rhombus has 2 pairs of parallel sides and 2 pairs of adjacent equal sides – he is still in the fourth generation.
[Place 2 arrows pointing down/right-left and the rhombus; at the height of the 4th generation card]

The member that we talk about now is a member that comes in the fifth general and has characteristics from the rhombus and the rectangle: the square. The square we can think of it as the perfect quadrilateral.
[Place 2 arrows pointing down/right-left and the square; at the height of the 5th generation card]
If the child had brought all the quadrilaterals, the guide can invite them to place them together with the other trapezium/kite.

When we distinguish the triangles we use adjectives (E.g. right-angled triangle, equilateral), in the case of the quadrilaterals we have new names to distinguish them.

blocks.text: The guide brings the presentation tray with the fundamental figures and takes out the insets for the triangle and square and the frame for the circle leaving the circle inset in the tray

The guide brings the metal inset for the triangle and for the square and makes sure that the child understands that they are the same things
The guide takes the triangle and places it in the circle frame
The guide continues doing the same with the rest of the polygons, in silence and with gentle movements.
The guide asks the child at the end what does he see
The child says that the space which is free is less and less
The guide says, “That is right, but imagine a polygon with 11 sides, 20 sides, 30 sides, 100 sides, 500.000 sides or 1 million sides.”
The guide asks what happens with the length of the sides
The child says it is getting smaller
The guide says if we imagine this polygon with an infinite number of sides, each getting smaller and smaller.
The guide asks what did we reach – and brings the circle
The guide says that the circle is the limit of the regular polygons.

children.title: Follow-up activities
The story of the infinite numbers

blocks.text: The guide invites the children to think of numbers of circles in the geometry tray. How many circles do we have?
The children say six
The guide says that was easy to count. Let us think of a tea spoon of sand, if we put it on the table, after a lot of work could we count all the grains
f sand?
The children say that it will take a long time but it is possible
The guide says that’s true. If we want to count all the grains of sand on a long beach, could we do that?
The children say that it can take all our life

The guide says that’s true, when a number is too big to count it, we call it infinity. The mathematician John Wallis in the 16th century made a symbol for this quantity too big to count: the infinity symbol ∞
The guide can show the children a card with the symbol and how to draw it.

The guide continues by saying that the infinity symbol looks like a horizontal version of number 8 and it represents the concept of eternity, endless and unlimited. Some scientists say, however, that John Wallis could have taken the Greek lowercase letter ω “omega” as a source for creating the infinity sign. Omega in Greek means great so maybe John Wallis thought that it is a good letter to express such a big number that it cannot it even be read.

children.title: Presentation of the “2nd Stage: Formulae”
Review the relationships between the 2 circles

blocks.text: The guide brings the circles and reviews the relationships between two circles.
The guide invites the child to find the radius for both circles by first finding the diameters of the circles and after the radii.
The guide places the circles on the board with the radii visible
The guide takes two radii and places them on top of the circles. He asks the children what the sticks represent.
The child says the 2 radii

children.title: Externally tangent

blocks.text: The guide says it is the sum of the two radii so we can write (R + r) on blank slips under the radii
The guide places the slips on the right of the board and says that we are interested in the distances between the centers
The guide places the two circles externally tangent. He places his fingers and asks if the distance between the centers of two externally tangent circles is …
The child says equal to the sum of the radii
The guide writes d = (R+r) with slips of paper – we can call it a formulae

children.title: External

blocks.text: The guide places the two circles external. He places his fingers and asks if the distance between the centers of two external circles is …
The child says greater to the sum of the radii
The guide writes d > (R+r) with slips of paper – we can call it a formulae

children.title: Internally tangent

blocks.text: The guide places the two upper sticks on top of each other and says this is the difference of the radii so we can write (R-r)
The guide places the two circles internally tangent. He places his fingers and asks if the distance between the centers of two internally tangent circles is …
The child says equal to the difference of the radii
The guide writes d = (R-r) with slips of paper – we can call it a formulae

children.title: Internal

blocks.text: The guide places the two circles internal. He places his fingers and asks if the distance between the centers of two internal circles is …
The child says smaller to the difference of the radii
The guide writes d < (R-r) with slips of paper – we can call it formulae.

children.title: Concentric

blocks.text: The guide places the two circles concentric. He places his fingers and asks if the distance between the centers of two concentric circles is …
The child says that they coincide, so it is 0
The guide writes d = 0 with slips of paper – we can call it a formulae

children.title: Intersecting

blocks.text: The guide places the two circles externally tangent and places the radii.
The guide reviews the distance between the two centers is equal to the sum of the radii
The guide says that today we are interested in intersecting circles. The guide places the circles intersecting and their radii.
He places his fingers and asks if the distance between the centers of two intersecting circles is …
The child says it is less than the sum of the radii.
The guide writes d < (R+r) with slips of paper
The guide says that this not enough, it helps us but let’s see what happens when we place the circles internally tangent
The guide places the circles internally tangent
The child says that the distance is equal to the difference of the radii
The places the circles intersecting, he places his fingers and asks if the distance between the centers of two intersecting circles is …
The child says that it is greater than the difference of the radii
The guide says than we discovered two parts of the formulae. Let us put them together.
The child places d < (R+r) and d > (R-r).
The guide invites the child to read the last one in reverse
The child reads (R-r) < d
The guide suggests to put the two parts of the formulae together
The child forms (R-r) < d < (R+r)

children.title: Congruence, similarity and equivalence
Introduction and description of the material

blocks.text: This work can be initiated while still working with the Quadrilaterals or Polygons. Two figures are congruent when they are identical in all the aspects, the same shape and the same size. Two figures are similar when they have the same shape but different size. Two figures are equivalent when they have the same value (size) but different shape. The materials used for this chapter are mainly the divided figures: the divided triangles, the divided squares and the divided circles. These figures have their origins in the Children’s House in the Geometry cabinet.
Triangles
4 frames with the equilateral triangle from frame 1 divided in 2, 3 and 4 triangles
Frame 1: 1 Equilateral triangle- the side of 10 cm
Frame 2: 2 Right-angled scalene triangles with the sides of 10 cm (Hypotenuse), 5cm (Short leg), 8.6602... cm (Long leg) ℎ = √3 × s 2
Frame 3: 3 Obtuse-angled isosceles triangles with the sides of 10 cm, 10 cm, 6.(666) cm (Long leg) - Radius = 2/3 height
Frame 4: 4 Equilateral triangles with the sides of 5 cm
Squares
9 frames with the square from frame 1 divided in 2, 4 and 8, 16 triangles and 2, 4, 8, 16 rectangles
Frame 1: 1 Square - the side of 10 cm
Frame 2: 2 Rectangles with the sides of 5cm and 10 cm
Frame 3: 4 Squares with the sides of 5cm and 5 cm
Frame 4: 8 Rectangles with the sides of 5cm and 2.5 cm
Frame 5: 16 Squares with the sides of 2.5cm and 2.5 cm
Frame 6: 2 Right-angled isosceles triangles with the sides of 10 cm (Legs), 10cm (Leg), 14.14213... cm (hypotenuse) 𝑑 = √2 × s
Frame 7: 4 Right-angled isosceles triangles with the sides of 5 cm
Frame 8: 8 Right-angled isosceles triangles with the sides of 5 cm
Frame 9: 16 Right-angled isosceles triangles with the sides of 5 cm
Circles
10 frames with the circle from frame 1 divided in 2, 3 … 10 sectors
Frame 1: 1 Circle - the diameter of 10 cm
Frame 2: 2 Semi-circles
Frame 3: 3 Sectors (3 radii)
Frame 4: 4 Sectors (4 radii)
Frame 5: 5 Sectors (5 radii)
Frame 6: 6 Sectors (6 radii)
Frame 7: 7 Sectors (7 radii)
Frame 8: 8 Sectors (8 radii)
Frame 9: 9 Sectors (9 radii)
Frame 10: 10 Sectors (10 radii)
= “May I have a large container of coffee” = 3.1415926

children.title: Finding the area of the common parallelogram (later work)

blocks.text: The guide takes the green right-angled triangle and uses it as a measure tool to show that the length of the long leg is equal to the length of the long side of the rectangle but also to the length of the height of the common parallelogram. The length of the short leg of the triangle is equal to the length of the short side of the rectangle but also to the length of the short side of the common parallelogram. As we know that the area of the rectangle is the length of the long side multiplied by the length of the short side, therefore the area of the common parallelogram is the length of the height multiplied by the length of the short side.

Finding and identifying the 3 equilateral triangles
Find the 3 equilateral triangles and name them T1, T2, T3

blocks.text: The guide looks in the 3 boxes and finds the 3 equilateral triangles(grey, red and yellow from the triangular box and small hexagonal box)
The guide says that he wants to give names to the triangles
The guide says the grey one is T1, the yellow is T2 and the small red one is T3
The guide invites the child to place slips with the names on them

children.title: Finding the value relationship of T1 and T2
Explore the value relationship of T1 and T2

blocks.text: The guide looks at T2 and T1 and says that he wants to find the value relationship
The guide says that we can use what’s in the boxes to explore Child can use helpers to explore
The children start exploring.
The child can make T1 from 4 equilateral triangles and can make a trapezium from 3 green equilateral triangles to find the relationship
The child concludes that T1 has a value of 3/4 of T2 therefore T2 has a value of 4/3 of T1

Another way is to use the 2 green halves for T1 and 3 red obtuse-angled triangles for T2 – he can flip the green triangles to form a kite – and from superimposing the red triangles the child can see that 1 fourth is missing from the kite therefore T2 is 3/4 of T1 and T1 is 4/3 of T2

The child can find that the height of T1 is 3/4 of its own side.
The guide can invite the child to explore the same equivalence with the metal insets

children.title: Finding the difference between T1 and T2

blocks.text: The guide looks at T2 and T1 and says that he wants to find the difference between T1 and T2. He invites the child to use mediators, the 4 equilateral triangles for T1 and the 3 green equilateral triangles in the shape of a trapezium

The guide can show to the child that T1 – T2 = T3. He invites the child play around with the terms to see what he discovers
The child does T2 + T3 = T1

children.title: Superimposing T2 over T1

blocks.text: The child also find out that by superimposing T2 to T1 the difference is an isosceles trapezium equivalent to T3
The child also moves T2 to the base of T1 and find out that the difference is a concave hexagon
The child can place T2 in the middle of T1 and find out that the difference is a triangular figure
The child can also tilt T2 so that T1 – T2 are 3 obtuse-angled scalene triangles.

Introduction

blocks.text: This material consists of insets and frames. The material was mentioned by Maria Montessori in the Advanced Montessori Method Vol. 2, which was published in 1916.
The insets are divided into families. There are seven families.
This material was initially used for equivalence and area, later Maria Montessori divided introduced the yellow material for the work with area.
The first shape is the first term of comparison, and the rectangle it is the second term of comparison.
Maria Montessori in her choice for the shapes in the inset always chooses the special shapes: equilateral triangle, rhombus made from 2 equilateral triangles, equilateral trapezium.

children.title: Area

blocks.text: We can think of the area as the size of a surface. As we have to find the size, it is like getting to the etymology of the word geometry- “land/earth measurement”. The children have already explored the congruence, similarity or equivalence but they never explored how large a figure is. They have been indirectly prepared in arithmetic and in geometry for this work so they can really understand it.

The numerical value tells us how much space a figure occupies – there is a universal aspect and a cultural specific aspect (e.g., Italy uses square meters meanwhile England square feet - feet, meters being the cultural aspect and square the universal aspect). In the work here, the introduction the unit for 1 dimension was stick of 1, which was 2 cm, for area the square of 2 cm2 and for volume a cube of 2 cm3.
The rectangle is chosen as the first figure for the calculations of area as the rectangle can fit the square inside perfectly.

The children can continue playing either in the same way or by starting from the formula.
Final observations

The children have been prepared for this work for a long time with practical life activities such as washing a table, the metal insets. The surface has been presented as a fundamental concept and with the work for area the child attaches an arithmetical value to that concept.

The rectangle is the point of reference for area as it contains the square. In the yellow material for area only 3 figures have been chosen for the work with area: rectangle, common parallelogram and the triangles.
Whenever the mediator is brought, it has to be first a check for congruence.

blocks.text: The guide brings the regular decagon from the geometry cabinet and reviews the parts.
The guide asks the child if we can find the perimeter of the decagon
The child says that we can measure one side and multiply it by 10
The guide brings the circle and reviews the parts.
The guide asks the child he can find the circumference of the circle
The child says that the side is a point and there are too many to count.

children.title: Use a string to find the circumference

blocks.text: The guide says what we can do is to do what the people did many years ago: wrap a string around the circle and find how long it. When we straighten out the circumference, we can say we rectified it.
The guide invites the child to choose other circles and try by himself.
The child tries

children.title: Mark the circle, roll it, mark the starting and end points

blocks.text: The guide says that the people also used another method. The guide marks the circle and rolls the circle on the board. He marks from where it started and where it finished and at the end draws a line.
The guide invites the child to work in the same way writing which circle it is on the left side.
The guide says that someone had made a brilliant discovery: the diameter
f the circle was contained in the circumference 3 times and a little bit
more. The mathematicians of that time wanted to find out how much was that bit.
The guide invites the child to write on tickets C = d x 3 approx.

The guide says that in the Old Testament we can read how he was building a palace and he made 2 great round basins of metals – 10 cubits from brim to brim and with a circumference of 30 cubits. So we can see that this first knowledge was there a long long time ago.

The guide takes a piece of paper and marks the bit at the end of the line drawn by the circle with the circumference of 10. He wants to see how many times this little bit from the end will fit in the circumference. It fitted 7 times and a bit so now we can say that the C = d x 3 1/7 approx.
The guide uses the ruler in order to find out in millimeters how much that 1/7 is. The guide says that it is more than 14 and less than 15. So we can write C = d x 3.14 approx.

The guide continues saying that the mathematicians were not happy with that. They understood that the diameter had always to be multiplied by the same constant number – it must be a special number, so let us give it a name. The name that the Greeks used for that is periferia so why not use the letter in the Greek alphabet for that:
The guide shows to the children how to write it and how to replace it in the formula. C = d x
The guide says that we can write our formula like C = by replacing the d with 2r
We can also have presentations for finding the areas of each surface part
f the circle: segment, sector and annulus.
Finding the circumference of a circle
8 -12 years old

children.title: Volume

blocks.text: If the area tells the size of the surface then volume tells the size of the solid or how much space it occupies. Finding the volume is attaching a numerical value to a solid. The children have this experience from working with the golden bead material and later in elementary in the work of building equivalent figures with the cubes. The work that the children have done with the area is a key for the work that the children will do with the volume. Working with the volume shows the importance of all the indirect preparation that has been done before. The mind has absorbed the information and the impressions that are critical in the work that they are doing now.
Outline
Finding the volume of the guide solid
Finding the volume of the other prisms
Finding the volume of the pyramids
Finding the volume of the cylinder and cone
Finding lateral and total surface area
Finding the volume of the sphere (not done in this course)

The guide chooses a sector made of 3 pieces of 1/10 and 2 pieces of 1/20. He says that he wants to find the area of this sector. The guide invites the child to inspect the parts of the sector
The child looks and identifies 2 radii and 1 arc.
The guide says that we are going to use “r” for the radius and “l” for the length of the arc.
The guide asks the child if he remembers how to transform this pieces into a rectangle as he did before with the all the pieces of the circle
The child forms a rectangle.
The guide invites the child to identify the base and the height of the rectangle formed.
The child says that the height is the radius “r” and the base is half the length of the arc “l/2”.
The guide invites the child to write the formula for the area that he discovered
The child writes A sector = l/2 x r

children.title: Finding the LSA of the cone [not done in class]

blocks.text: The guide says that now we know how to find the surface of a sector. Let us write what we know about this sector.
The child says this is a sector of a circle with the radius equal to the slant height and with an arc equal to the circumference of the base of the cone.
The guide asks the child if he remembers how to calculate the area of a sector
The child says A sector = l/2 x r where l is the length of the arc of the sector.
The guide invites the child to place in the formula the things that we know.
The child writes LSA = 2 r/2 x SH; LSA = SH x x r
The child says that to find the TSA we just have to add the Abase therefore TSA = (SH x x r) + r2

children.title: Conclusion for Geometry

blocks.text: The Montessori approach for Geometry it is remarkable for the use of the materials to help the children understand the concepts, think and discover through manipulation.
The geometry becomes psychogeometry as it is presented according to the developmental needs of the child in the second plane.
The difficulties are isolated and worked one at a time allowing the child to focus
n a certain aspect. It permits the child to repeat with variety and use the
concepts learned and discovered repeatedly as the work progresses.
The work is a synthesis of knowledge allowing the children to work further and make their own discoveries.

Coming back to the materials, it is very important to make clear that the materials are an aid to development and the children are free to abandon them as soon as they extracted the knowledge. The great mathematicians at the beginnings of their work have always used materials to discover the new concepts and to create an order in their mind through the physical manipulation.

The role of the materials is to help the children understand much more than can a teacher transmit through an abstract lesson. The manipulation of the material creates a habit for discovery. It supports the hungry mind of the child in the second plane of development, a hungry mind that should stay with the human beings through their entire life.
The work that the children do in a Montessori environment prepares the mind of the child. It helps them to be more observant, critical thinkers and to understand more.
